scholar: J. H. Bernard (Archbishop of Dublin, d. 1927; completed by A. H. McNeile)

chapter_or_section: Commentary on John 8:58-59 ('Before Abraham was, I AM')
quote_orig: It is clear that Jn. means to represent Jesus as thus claiming for Himself the timeless being of Deity, as distinct from the temporal existence of man. [...] but here (and at 13:19) Jesus Himself is reported as having said I (am) He, which is a definite assertion of His Godhead, and was so understood by the Jews.
context_before: Bernard has just said that absolute ego eimi, with no predicate, 'is the equivalent of the solemn' Hebrew formula, 'I (am) He, which is the self-designation of Yahweh in the prophets.' He notes a similar use at 13:19 (superscript reference in print).
what_it_says: Bernard says John presents Jesus as claiming the timeless being of Deity, and that Jesus is reported as saying 'I (am) He', which he calls a definite assertion of his Godhead, understood as such by the Jews.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus himself speaks as YHWH / claims divine identity, as Bernard reads the Gospel report; also (B) the Gospel portrayal
scholar_qualification: Bernard frames it as what John 'means to represent' and what Jesus 'is reported' as saying, i.e. a claim as the Gospel presents it; he does not say the historical Jesus spoke these exact words. Limits elsewhere in the same commentary: at 10:30 he rejects the reading of 'identity of' substance (p. 366), and on 10:33 he says 'Jesus never called Himself "son of Yahweh"' (p. 368).
limits: Read from archive.org OCR and checked against the page image (PDF page 40). Superscript verse numbers and the Greek are printed as colon-separated numbers here; the 'I (am) He' printed form was confirmed on the image. Bernard is 1929 and older than the current scholarly consensus on Johannine Christology; he is cited as a classic, not current.

chapter_or_section: Commentary on John 10:31 (Jews take up stones)
quote_orig: The Jewish opponents of Jesus, with a true instinct, perceived that He was claiming to be more than human, [...] They fetched stones from a distance, that they might stone Him.
context_before: The paragraph before concerns Jesus' words at 10:30 ('I and the Father are one'), which Bernard reads as unity of will and purpose, not of substance. The 10:31 comment then opens with the Jews' attempt to stone Jesus, followed by Bernard's own judgment of their reading.
what_it_says: Bernard says the Jewish opponents correctly understood Jesus to claim more than a human status, and that they took up stones on that basis.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus claims to be more than human (Bernard's words); (B) the Gospel's portrayal. Bernard does not use the word 'divine' here.
scholar_qualification: This is Bernard's reading of the opponents' understanding, endorsed as 'a true instinct'. He does NOT read 10:30 as identity of substance (see K3-10, p. 366), and he limits the title 'Son of God' (p. 368).
limits: Read from archive.org OCR (PDF page 84 text layer). The Greek lemma between the two English sentences is omitted and marked [...]. Not checked against the image.

work: 'A Narrative Analysis of Mark's Use of the Shema', Perichoresis 24.1 (2026): 56-72
edition: Emanuel University of Oradea, Perichoresis 24.1, 2026; open-access journal (DOI 10.2478/perc-2026-0004)
chapter_or_section: Section 'The Messiah Son of the Blessed One: Mark 14:61-62'
quote_orig: Now, ego eimi can be used as nothing more than a phrase of identification (e.g. Matthew 26:22), but it must also be recognized that there are contexts where an implication of deity is present (John 8:58) and others in which it is at least strongly suggested (John 18:5–6).
context_before: Hicks follows Marcus (1989) in reading the high priest's 'Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?' as restrictive, so that Jesus is the Messiah who claims to be 'Son of God'. 'This would give important context for Jesus' answer to the high priest, especially his first two words: "I am" (ego eimi).'
what_it_says: Hicks argues that ego eimi in Mark 14:62 is an 'exegetically loaded' context where deity may be implied, though he grants it can be a mere identification.
claim_supported: (B) the Gospel writer portrays Jesus as sharing YHWH's identity (Hicks's main thesis); (A) only as a hedged possibility for the words of Jesus himself
scholar_qualification: Hicks's thesis is about Mark's narrative: the abstract says 'the Gospel writer utilized the Shema within his narrative to express an early high Christology'. He poses the key question as open ('Does this context suggest a claim for divinity or is it simply an expression of self-identification?'), and on the same page says 'Jesus' claim to be the Son of Man ... could also be seen as a claim to deity' (hedged). He does not claim that the historical Jesus used these words as a claim to deity. Hicks treats Marcus's 'quasi-divine agent' reading as the rival.
limits: Read from the PDF text layer and the journal's own page numbers (PDF page 13 = journal p. 68; offset 55). Article is a 2026 journal article, not a monograph. Its claim is about Mark's Christology; it is cited here as scholarly support for claim (B), not as a historical-Jesus claim.
